site.title: Why keep a promise that no longer pays?
site.description: An illustrated film you scroll through: why people keep promises that no longer pay, from the prisoner’s dilemma to Vanberg’s experiment (2008).
finding.description: Why a lab session cannot tell personal guilt from partner-specific commitment, and what comparing worlds with different background trust shows.

sources.axelrod-hamilton-1981: The payoffs of the prisoner’s dilemma, and the condition that cooperating every round pays more than taking turns at defecting; also the chance that the same two meet again, and the tournament that Tit-for-Tat won.
sources.at.axelrod-hamilton-1981: Figure 1 and its caption, and the chance of meeting again, p. 1392; the tournament, p. 1393; note 17, p. 1396.
sources.case-2017: The place to play the repeated dilemma.
sources.vanberg-2008: The game in which only one person decides, the partner switch that tells the two reasons apart, and the article’s conclusion, which the film paraphrases.
sources.vanberg-payoffs: The payoffs of the decision: what the one who decides gets for keeping the money or rolling the die, and what the one who receives gets from each face.
sources.at.vanberg-payoffs: Supplement A, p. 2, table “Payoffs From the Decision”.
sources.vanberg-beliefs: What the recipients who held a promise bet that the one deciding would roll, without a switch and with one, on a five-point scale.
sources.at.vanberg-beliefs: The data, switch.dat, with the method of promises.do; the scale, Supplement B, pp. 2–3, Screen 5B.
sources.vanberg-design: How many people played the partner-switch game, and over how many rounds.
sources.at.vanberg-design: The data, switch.dat; the rounds, Supplement A, p. 1.
sources.vanberg-rates: How often the die was rolled after a promise, with the same partner and with a new partner promised by someone else.
sources.at.vanberg-rates: The data, switch.dat, counted with the method of promises.do.
sources.vanberg-procedure: The whole design: the rounds, a new partner in each, the one round that is paid, the roles drawn again, the chat’s turns, both chats after a switch and what the one who receives sees.
sources.at.vanberg-procedure: Supplement A, pp. 1–2; Supplement B, pp. 1–3.
sources.vanberg-guessing: What the guesses paid, in cents, to the one who receives and to the one who decides.
sources.at.vanberg-guessing: Supplement B, pp. 2–3, Screens 5B and 6A; Supplement A, p. 2.
sources.vanberg-cells: Every cell of the partner-switch treatment: how often the die was rolled, and what the dictators believed their partner expected.
sources.at.vanberg-cells: The data, switch.dat, blocks TABLE I to TABLE III of promises.do.
sources.vanberg-baseline: The two simpler treatments, with the chat and without it.
sources.at.vanberg-baseline: The data, baseline.dat, block TABLE A1 of promises.do; the article’s Appendix A.
sources.vanberg-abstract: The first sentence of the article’s abstract, quoted.
sources.charness-dufwenberg-2006: Guilt aversion: the voice of what the other expects.
sources.battigalli-dufwenberg-2007: Guilt aversion: the voice of what the other expects.
sources.vanberg-second-order: The belief that a promise will be kept, which the curve holds fixed: the mean second-order belief of the dictators without a partner switch, what they believed their partner expected.
sources.at.vanberg-second-order: The data, switch.dat, block TABLE I of promises.do.
sources.kawagoe-narita-2014: Personal guilt: letting down an expectation hurts only if you created it, so after a partner switch it is zero.
sources.curve: The curve: in each world of background trust, what each of the three reasons earns and where personal guilt rolls, as the engine measured it.
sources.at.curve: The curve the engine exports, copied into this site unchanged.
sources.curve-finding: What the page on the finding derives from the curve: the guilt available, the threshold it must pass, the analytic cut and the robustness variant. θ and c are given, and explained, only on that page.
sources.at.curve-finding: The same curve: the guilt available in each row, θ and c, and the robustness variant.

film.label: The film
film.arrival.ask: “Will you promise me you’ll roll the die?”
film.ticket.promise.detail: A thread ties you to the other
film.arrival.promised: You promised. A golden thread now ties you to the other, and it stays with you, top left.
film.arrival.refused: You promised nothing. No thread ties you to anyone.
film.arrival.noscript: Choosing needs JavaScript. The story goes on as if you had promised.
film.arrival.still: At dawn, across a table with a die floating above it, a square asks a circle, you, for a promise; a golden thread ties them.
film.chapter.heading: Chapter {n}: {title}
film.two-rooms.still: Two rooms with a wall between them: the circle, you, and the square, each under a hanging bulb. Above them, the prisoner’s dilemma board: {R} each if both cooperate, {P} each if both defect, and {T} against {S} if only one defects. Both defecting is marked as where both end up.
film.ticket.cooperate.detail: {R} if they cooperate · {S} if they defect
film.ticket.defect.detail: {T} if they cooperate · {P} if they defect
film.two-rooms.out.cooperate: You cooperated, and the other defected. You get {you}; the other, {other}.
film.two-rooms.out.defect: You defected, and so did the other. You get {you}; the other, {other}.
film.two-rooms.noscript: Playing needs JavaScript. In the film the other always defects: if you cooperate, you get {S} and they get {T}; if you defect, you both get {P}.
film.two-rooms.ask.cooperate: If the other cooperates, what pays you more?
film.two-rooms.both: {move} pays you more in both columns: {a} against {b}, and {c} against {d}.
film.talk.still: Still in their rooms, the circle and the square talk over the wall in paper speech bubbles, under the prisoner’s dilemma board.
film.talk.opener: Hey… what are you going to do?
film.talk.noscript: Writing needs JavaScript. The story goes on as if you had promised, and the other had promised back.
film.fold.still: At noon, back at the table: the board has folded into a die, which rests on the table between the circle and the square.
film.fold.promised: You promised the other you’d roll the die.
film.ticket.roll.detail: You {roll} · the other {rollother}, unless a {failface} comes up
film.fold.out.roll: The die shows {face}: the other gets {other}. You keep {you}.
film.fold.out.fail: The die shows {face}: this time the other gets nothing. You keep {you}.
film.fold.out.cost: Rolling cost you {cost}; on average, it gives the other {expected}.
film.fold.noscript: Deciding needs JavaScript. These are the payoffs of the decision.
film.fold.table.caption: Payoffs of the decision
film.two-voices.still: In the early afternoon, back at the table, two voices float over the circle: a lilac cloud that keeps looking at the other, with the other’s face in its thought bubble, and a paper scroll sealed with the golden thread.
film.two-voices.says.expects: Roll just the same: the new partner expects the same, and doesn’t know about the switch.
film.two-voices.says.word: Roll less: you promised this person nothing.
film.blackout.still: In the afternoon, after the lights went out: a triangle sits in the square’s seat, across from the circle, and the golden thread still ties the circle to the square, who now stands farther off, at another table.
film.deck.message.1: Don’t worry. I’ll roll the die.
film.deck.message.6: Leave it to me: I’ll roll.
film.deck.out.kept: You roll the die for them: promise kept.
film.deck.out.rolled: You roll the die for them. You had promised them nothing.
film.deck.out.kept-money: You keep the {dont}. You had promised them nothing.
film.deck.tally: That was the deck. You kept {kept} of the {made} promises you made to the person across the table.
film.deck.swipe: Or swipe the card towards your choice.
film.deck.noscript: Deciding needs JavaScript. A different person waits on each card: with {same} of them you chatted and promised; with the other {switched}, the lights went out, and a new partner sat down holding a promise from someone else.
film.bet.label: How sure are you that the one who decides will roll?
film.bet.noscript: Betting needs JavaScript. The recipients in the experiment answered on a scale from “certainly rolls” to “certainly doesn’t roll”.
film.reveal.scale: What the recipients who held a promise bet, on average, on a scale read from {scalebottom} to {scaletop}
film.real-people.still: At sunset, back at the table, two paper signs hang over it: {rolledsame}% for the same partner and {rolledswitched}% for a new partner, each with a little cloud of what the recipients expected: {expectsame} and {expectswitched}.
film.real-people.guess.label: Your guess
film.my-research.still: At nightfall, under a paper lamp, a little paper engine with two gears sits on the table between the circle and the square, and the two voices look at it. Stars are out over the hills.
film.closing.still: At night, back at the first table under the paper lamp: the die floats over the table again between the circle and the square, the golden thread still ties them, and the two voices float over the circle. Stars are out over the hills.
film.closing.ask.promised: “You promised me you’d roll the die. Would you roll it now?”
film.closing.ask.refused: “You didn’t promise me anything. Would you roll the die now?”
film.closing.ask.unanswered: “You never answered me. Would you roll the die now?”
film.closing.out.roll: You’d roll it. The other smiles.
film.closing.out.dont: You’d keep the {dont}. The other doesn’t answer.
film.closing.noscript: Answering needs JavaScript. Whatever you would say, the film goes on.
film.closing.page.not.out: Then I owe you a few minutes. Thank you for staying to the end.
film.closing.page.noscript: Answering needs JavaScript. Either way, thank you for staying to the end.
